(or a with inline styles) that looks like a heading but carries no heading role, so screen-reader heading navigation and the document outline are broken; section structure is invisible to AT.
patterns.typicalMarkup:
Our Services

We offer ...
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: There is no heading element at all, so a linter sees only well-formed paragraph text with no rule violation (no empty heading, no skipped level). Deciding that a given bold/large paragraph is functioning as a heading requires reading the content and judging its role from visual prominence and meaning.
patterns.realWorldNote: TinyMCE/CKEditor accessibility guidance explicitly tells authors not to fake headings with bold/size and to use the format dropdown instead. https://www.tiny.cloud/blog/accessible-rich-text-editor/ and https://ckeditor.com/blog/how-to-make-a-website-accessible-step-by-step-guide/

patterns.platform: Shopify / WooCommerce / Magento product-variant color swatches
patterns.name: Color-only swatch with no text label or out-of-stock cue
patterns.description: Selectable variant swatches are rendered as colored squares/circles whose only differentiator is the fill color, with no accessible name for the color and no non-color indication of state. "Out of stock" or "unavailable" variants are signaled purely by graying-out, and the selected swatch is shown only by a subtle color/border change. Color-blind and screen-reader users cannot tell red from green, which swatch is chosen, or which are unavailable.
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: An empty <button> with no name may trip a 4.1.2 rule, but the use-of-color failure (state and meaning conveyed only by hue, no text/icon equivalent) is invisible to automation — tools cannot determine that color is the sole carrier of "selected"/"out of stock" or that two swatches are only distinguishable by hue. That is a visual-semantic call.
patterns.realWorldNote: Shopify/EAA swatch guidance and Bricks/Salesforce CC audits flag color-only swatches and out-of-stock graying as a11y problems requiring text labels. https://craftshift.com/shopify-european-accessibility-act-swatches/ and https://forum.bricksbuilder.io/t/accessibility-issue-with-color-variation-swatches-edited-new-issue/38992

patterns.platform: Material UI Snackbar / generic React toast libraries
patterns.name: Toast/snackbar fired outside a live region
patterns.description: A transient toast ("Item added to cart", "Saved", "Error: try again") is injected into the DOM as a styled <div> with no role="status"/role="alert" and not inside an aria-live region. Sighted users see it appear and fade; screen-reader users get no announcement at all, so success/error feedback is silently lost. Often compounded by auto-dismiss before any AT could reach it.
patterns.typicalMarkup: Item added to cart
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: The toast exists only momentarily and contains valid markup; static scanners audit a snapshot of the DOM and have no concept of "this content appeared dynamically and was not announced." Detecting it requires observing the runtime mutation and judging that it is a status message that needed a live region.
patterns.realWorldNote: Documented as a recurring toast failure; MUI Snackbar focus/announcement issues are tracked upstream. https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/accessible-notifications-with-aria-live-regions-part-1/ and https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/22354

patterns.platform: React / Vue / Angular SPA with client-side router (React Router, Vue Router)
patterns.name: <title> and focus never update on route change
patterns.description: Client-side navigation swaps the view in place without a full page load. document.title stays at the app's default, and focus remains wherever the user clicked, so screen-reader users hear no page-change announcement and keyboard users are stranded mid-page. The browser history changes but AT perceives nothing — the user has no idea they navigated or where they are.
patterns.typicalMarkup:
<!-- after navigating /home -> /checkout, title is unchanged -->
<head><title>My App</title></head>
<!-- new view rendered; no focus move, no title update -->
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan of any one route finds a present, non-empty <title>, so 2.4.2 passes per page. The failure is the absence of an update across a runtime navigation event — automation auditing one DOM state cannot observe that the title/focus failed to change on transition.
patterns.realWorldNote: Widely documented SPA failure mode; routers don't reset focus or title on navigation. https://kittygiraudel.com/2020/01/15/accessible-title-in-a-single-page-react-application/ and https://github.com/remix-run/react-router/discussions/9863

patterns.platform: Word / Google Docs paste into a CMS WYSIWYG (mso styles, layout tables)
patterns.name: Pasted Office HTML: layout tables and lost reading order
patterns.description: Pasting from Word/Google Docs carries over <table> elements used purely for visual layout (multi-column newsletters, side-by-side text/image), plus mso-* inline styling and empty/merged cells. AT announces "table, N columns, N rows" and reads cell-by-cell, scrambling the intended reading order; what was a two-column flyer becomes nonsensical when linearized.
patterns.typicalMarkup: Left column intro...Right column sidebar...
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: A layout table with no th and no scope can look identical to a legitimately simple table; tools cannot reliably decide whether a table is conveying tabular data or just positioning content, nor whether the linearized cell order reads sensibly. Distinguishing layout-vs-data and judging resulting reading order is a human semantic task.
patterns.realWorldNote: Office-paste artifacts (layout tables, jumbled reading order, headings tagged as paragraphs) are a documented conversion problem. https://www.section508.gov/training/documents/aed-cop-docx05/ and https://tlos.vt.edu/digital-accessibility/calm/check-reading-order.html

patterns.platform: Page builders using CSS flexbox/grid order (Elementor, Webflow, Bricks, custom responsive layouts)
patterns.name: Visual reorder via CSS order/row-reverse desyncs DOM/focus order
patterns.description: Designers rearrange columns/cards visually with flex order, order: -1, flex-direction: row-reverse, or grid placement while leaving DOM order untouched. The page looks correct, but keyboard Tab order and screen-reader reading order follow the (now-stale) DOM, so focus jumps erratically across the page and content is read in a sequence that doesn't match the visual layout. Especially common at the responsive breakpoint where source order was authored for desktop.
patterns.typicalMarkup:
Step 1
Step 2 (appears first visually)
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: DOM and focus order are technically valid and tools don't compute the rendered visual geometry to compare against tab sequence. Deciding that the visual order is meaningful (a sequence of steps) and therefore must match DOM order requires understanding content meaning and seeing the rendered layout.
patterns.realWorldNote: Classic Flexbox/Grid reorder pitfall affecting 1.3.2 and 2.4.3. https://wcag.dock.codes/documentation/wcag132/ and https://testparty.ai/blog/wcag-2-4-3-focus-order-2025-guide

patterns.platform: Multilingual sites / auto-translate widgets (Weglot, WPML, Google Website Translator)
patterns.name: Foreign-language passage with no lang, or stale html lang after translation
patterns.description: A page in one primary language embeds quotes, names, product blurbs, or whole machine-translated sections in another language without a lang attribute on those parts; or a translation layer swaps visible text but leaves <html lang="en"> unchanged. The screen reader reads French/Arabic/Japanese text with English phonetics (or vice versa), producing gibberish pronunciation. Often the page title/nav stays untranslated while the body is translated.
patterns.typicalMarkup: Our motto: Liberté, égalité, fraternité
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Tools verify that an html lang exists and that lang values are valid BCP-47 tags, but they cannot read the text and detect that a passage is in a different language than its declared lang, nor that the declared page language no longer matches the rendered (translated) content. That requires language identification of the visible text.
patterns.realWorldNote: Missing lang on parts / mismatched page lang causes screen readers to mispronounce; documented for multilingual sites. https://benmyers.dev/blog/multilingual-web-accessibility/ and https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/meaning-other-lang-id.html

patterns.platform: Theme components using icon fonts / inline SVG (Font Awesome, Bootstrap icons, Shopify Dawn header)
patterns.name: Icon-only button/link with no accessible name
patterns.description: A hamburger, search magnifier, close X, cart, or social-share control is rendered as a button/anchor whose only content is an <i> icon-font glyph or a decorative <svg> with no aria-label, no visually hidden text, and no title. Screen readers announce a bare "button" or "link" with no indication of what it does; voice-control users have nothing to target.
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one is largely catchable: axe/Lighthouse flag buttons and links with no accessible name. (Edge cases where an icon font ligature renders visible text the AT can read, or where a name exists but is wrong, still need human review, but the bare unnamed-control case is a reliable linter hit.)
patterns.realWorldNote: Icon-only controls are the canonical 4.1.2 "button with no accessible name" failure; Font Awesome's own docs and Shopify Dawn audits call it out. https://docs.fontawesome.com/web/dig-deeper/accessibility and https://testparty.ai/blog/shopify-dawn-theme-accessibility

patterns.platform: CMS list/grid widgets (WordPress blog loops, news cards, "recent posts")
patterns.name: Repeated "Read more" / "Learn more" links with no distinguishing purpose
patterns.description: A loop of post/product cards renders an identical generic call-to-action link under each item. When a screen-reader user pulls up the links list (or tabs through), they hear "Read more, link" / "Learn more, link" a dozen times with nothing to differentiate destinations. The descriptive context (the card heading) is programmatically separate from the link, so out of context the purpose is undeterminable.
patterns.typicalMarkup:
Spring Sale Tips

...

Read more

New Store Hours

...

Read more
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Each link has non-empty text, so it passes the "link must have text" rule. Some tools heuristically flag the literal strings "read more"/"click here", but they cannot judge whether programmatically-determined context (an ancestor heading, aria-describedby) makes the purpose clear, nor whether the destinations actually differ — that needs reading the page.
patterns.realWorldNote: Ambiguous "Read more"/"Learn more" link soup from CMS content is a textbook 2.4.4 failure. https://www.visionaustralia.org/business-consulting/digital-access/blog/how-to-make-read-more-links-accessible and https://theadminbar.com/accessibility-weekly/ambiguous-links/

patterns.platform: PDF-to-HTML export tools (Acrobat "Export as HTML", InDesign publish, pdf2htmlEX preserved-layout mode)
patterns.name: Absolutely-positioned spans replace semantic structure
patterns.description: "Preserved layout" conversion reproduces the PDF pixel-for-pixel by emitting hundreds of absolutely-positioned <span>/<div> elements, one per text run, with no headings, lists, or paragraphs — and DOM order driven by the PDF's internal object order, not reading order. Visually identical to the source, but linearized AT output is scrambled: column text interleaves, headings are plain spans, and there is no navigable structure.
patterns.typicalMarkup:
Annual
Report 2024
Revenue grew...
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Markup is valid; there are no missing alts or empty headings to flag. Tools don't reconstruct visual reading flow from absolute coordinates to detect that the DOM sequence diverges from the visual sequence, nor that prominent spans are functioning as headings. Reading order correctness and implied structure are human judgments.
patterns.realWorldNote: Preserved-layout PDF-to-HTML uses absolutely-positioned spans that destroy semantic structure and reading order. https://www.chhs.colostate.edu/accessibility/best-practices-how-tos/pdf-converted/ and conversion-tool comparisons noting preserved vs reflowable trade-offs.

patterns.platform: RTL-language sites / themes not built for bidi (Arabic/Hebrew/Persian on LTR-first templates)
patterns.name: Missing or mismatched dir causing broken bidirectional text
patterns.description: An RTL-language page is served on a template that only sets <html lang> (or sets neither dir nor a matching lang), so dir defaults to ltr. Mixed Arabic+English or Hebrew+numerals render with mangled visual order (punctuation on the wrong side, embedded LTR runs misplaced), and the lang/dir mismatch means AT cannot apply correct directionality or pronunciation. The page may look mostly right to a casual sighted skim but reads incoherently.
patterns.typicalMarkup: اشترِ iPhone 15 الآن
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Tools can check that lang exists but rarely flag a missing dir, and they cannot evaluate whether the rendered bidirectional sequence is correct or whether embedded LTR runs need isolation. Judging that the visual/reading sequence of bidi text is broken requires reading the script and seeing the render.
patterns.realWorldNote: Missing/incorrect dir breaks RTL display and accessibility; the HTML attribute is required even if CSS sets direction. https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-html-dir and https://accessibility-test.org/blog/support/rtl-right-to-left-website-accessibility-considerations/

patterns.platform: Marketing hero banners / promo slides in CMS slideshows (Shopify slideshow, Squarespace banner, email-style heroes)
patterns.name: Headline baked into a hero image (image of text)
patterns.description: The campaign headline, price, and CTA wording are composited into a single hero JPG/PNG by a designer, then placed with a generic or empty alt. The visible "text" pixelates on zoom, can't be restyled for users who need larger/high-contrast type, and is either unreadable to AT (empty alt) or crammed into one alt string. Often the same banner is the page's only H1-level content, so the heading is also an image.
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: An empty-alt decorative image passes 1.1.1 trivially, and a non-empty alt passes too — tools cannot OCR the image to discover it contains essential text that should have been live HTML, nor judge whether that text is "essential" (logo) versus avoidable. Detecting text-in-image and deciding it's a 1.4.5 violation is a visual/semantic call.
patterns.realWorldNote: Compositing headline text into hero images is a documented 1.4.5 failure; fix is extracting to HTML/CSS overlay. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/images-of-text.html and https://testparty.ai/blog/wcag-1-4-5-images-of-text-2025-guide

patterns.platform: Page-builder custom widgets (Elementor/WPBakery div "buttons", custom controls with aria-label)
patterns.name: div role=button whose accessible name contradicts its visible label
patterns.description: A builder renders an interactive control as a <div>/<span> with role="button" (or no role at all) and an aria-label that was authored separately from the visible text — so the on-screen label says "Submit" while the accessible name is "Send form", or the visible text is "Get Quote" but aria-label is "button". Voice-control users saying the visible word can't activate it, and screen-reader users hear something different from what's shown; when role is missing entirely, it isn't even reachable by keyboard.
patterns.typicalMarkup:
Submit
Get Quote
patterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: When an aria-label is present the control HAS an accessible name, so 4.1.2 "has a name" passes; comparing that name against the visible rendered text to detect a mismatch requires OCR/text extraction of the visible label and a semantic equality judgment that automation doesn't make reliably. (The pure missing-role/not-focusable variant is more linter-catchable.)
patterns.realWorldNote: div role=button with aria-label diverging from visible text is the canonical accessible-name-mismatch failure (also a 2.5.3 issue). https://www.makethingsaccessible.com/guides/say-what-you-see-wcag-2-5-3-label-in-name-level-a/ and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/failures/F96.html
